basics.name: Mechanism design apps: MotionGen (Pro), Linkage (Mechanism Designer and Simulator), PMKS+ (Planar Mechanism Kinematic Simulator Plus) and Gear Generator 3 (geargenerator.com)
basics.url: MotionGen: https://motiongen.io/ (web app) with info pages at https://www.stonybrook.edu/commcms/motiongen/; Linkage: https://blog.rectorsquid.com/linkage-mechanism-designer-and-simulator/ (download https://blog.rectorsquid.com/download-linkage/, samples https://blog.rectorsquid.com/sample-linkage-mechanisms-2/, help https://www.rectorsquid.com/Linkage/index.html); PMKS+: https://pmksplus.com/ (app https://app.pmksplus.com/, source https://github.com/PMKS-Web/PMKSWeb); Gear Generator: https://geargenerator.com/ (manual https://geargenerator.com/help.html)
basics.resource_type: interactive tool (four free design-and-animate apps: three planar linkage simulators and one gear-train designer)
basics.cost: MotionGen: free to use in the browser (Stony Brook page: 'Use it for free at motiongen.io'); the app has accounts, teacher classes and licences and links to paid SnappyXO hardware kits, so some classroom features may be paid [uncertain]; mobile app free on iOS/Android. Linkage: free Windows download (donations via PayPal/Patreon). PMKS+: free and open source. Gear Generator 3: free to design and animate; file exports (SVG/DXF/STL/OBJ) need a paid time-limited 'export pass' (in 2020 this was a USD 2 PayPal payment for 24 hours of DXF downloads, per a Model Engineer forum post; current price not checked [uncertain]). The desktop build of Gear Generator has no store
basics.license: MotionGen: proprietary, '(c) Mechanismic Inc. 2017-2023' in the app code; content all rights reserved [uncertain]. Linkage: 'protected by the WTFPL license' plus the author's extra terms (don't sell it, don't redistribute it from other sites for clickbait); source code available on request for non-commercial reasons. PMKS+: MIT License (README), so code and example linkages can be reused with attribution. Gear Generator 3: proprietary, '(C) 2014-2026 Gear Generator 3 - Created by Abel Vincze'; the page refuses to run inside another site's frame, so link to it rather than embed it. Files you design and export in any of them are your own designs
basics.language: English (all four). Gear Generator's author is Hungarian (iparigrafika.hu) but the app and manual are in English
basics.year: MotionGen: mobile app published 2016 (ASME IDETC 2016 paper, J. Mechanisms and Robotics 2017), web 'Pro' version later; code copyright 2017-2023. Linkage: author's blog archive goes back to 2010, current version 3.16.42, Mac port posts in June and September 2026 (start year of the program itself not confirmed [uncertain]). PMKS+: based on the older PMKS from Oregon State University; WPI student contributors from 2019 to 2025, package version 2.0.3 built on Angular 22 (so updated in 2026). Gear Generator: 2014 to 2026, now at version 3 (reads Gear Generator 2 files)
basics.access_barrier: MotionGen: none to open, runs in the browser; account sign-up exists for saving/classes (whether saving needs a free login not confirmed [uncertain]). Linkage: desktop install, Windows only (Windows XP build runs in Wine on Linux; Mac users need Parallels; native Mac version is a preview). PMKS+: none, runs in any browser. Gear Generator: none to design (browser, autosaves locally); paid pass to export files; its 3D view needs WebGL2
basics.image_license: MotionGen, Linkage and Gear Generator screenshots and videos: all rights reserved [uncertain], but images of your own designs exported from the apps are yours. PMKS+: MIT for the code; screenshots not separately licensed [uncertain]. Linkage sample videos are on the author's YouTube channel
basics.authority_level: MotionGen: academic peer-reviewed (Stony Brook University mechanical engineering, Prof. Anurag Purwar and Prof. Jeff Ge, NSF STTR funding; algorithms published in ASME journals) with a university spin-off company (Mechanismic Inc.). PMKS+: academic/educator (Worcester Polytechnic Institute students and faculty, verified with a MATLAB six-bar check). Linkage: single hobbyist/professional software developer (David Rector), community-trusted but unvetted. Gear Generator: single developer (Abel Vincze), unvetted but its manual cites ISO 606, DIN 6885 and ISO 4032 and explains its geometry openly

coverage.covers: MotionGen: planar N-bar linkages with revolute (pin) and prismatic (slider) joints, one or more degrees of freedom; four-bar motion synthesis from 3-5 poses; AI-driven path synthesis; library of four-bar (RRRR, RRRP, RRPR), six-bar (Watt I, Watt II, Stephenson I, II, III) and eight-bar linkages; rotary and linear actuators; slotted links; 2D and 3D views. Linkage: any configuration of links, pivoting and sliding connectors, rotary and linear (hydraulic-style) inputs, circular gears and chains (gears on moving links allowed), spline cams; about 50 downloadable sample mechanisms, with samples and screenshots showing (for example) Paddington rolling bridge, Hoberman circle, grasshopper beam engine, Theo Jansen leg, Klann linkage, Watt linkage, Whitworth quick-return speed-changing oscillator, level-moving table, link and sliding apertures, front-end loader, backhoe). PMKS+: planar linkages with revolute and prismatic joints (one slider at a time), welded links, kinematic analysis (position, velocity, acceleration graphs) and static/dynamic force analysis, four-bar synthesis from 3 coupler poses; example library (four-bar, slider-crank, Watt I, Watt II, Stephenson III). Gear Generator 3: involute spur, helical, double-helical and herringbone gears, internal (ring) gears, racks, planetary sets (with input/fixed/drive/output roles, so it can model a differential), ISO 606 chain sprockets and timing-belt pulleys (GT2 2 mm and 3 mm, HTD 3M/5M/8M, T5, T10), multi-stage gear trains on shared axles, profile shift, backlash and lost-motion simulation, tooth forces
coverage.organisation: Tools, not catalogues: each opens on a blank canvas plus an example library. MotionGen organises its library by linkage family (four-, six-, eight-bar, then Watt/Stephenson types), which needs vocabulary; its Stony Brook pages and video playlist explain the controls. Linkage has a sample page (one entry per mechanism with a file and a video) and a help site with a glossary. PMKS+ has a short 'Linkage Library (Example Linkages)'. Gear Generator is organised as a tree (each gear hangs off a parent by 'mesh' or 'axle') with a thorough manual (quick start, recipes such as 'a two-stage reducer', warnings table, reference card), the most beginner-readable of the four
coverage.scope_match: medium: they are tools rather than catalogues, but they cover in-scope families (linkages, motion converters like slider-cranks, quick-return and cams, and especially gear trains: planetary, rack, chain and belt drives, multi-stage reducers) and let a beginner see and test a mechanism before making it. They do not cover connections, latches, torque limiting or adhesives
coverage.taxonomy_used: MotionGen: kinematic chain types (four-bar with RRRR/RRRP/RRPR joint strings; six-bar Watt I/II and Stephenson I/II/III; eight-bar) and dyad types (RR, PR, RP). PMKS+: same Watt/Stephenson naming for its examples, joints split into revolute, prismatic and welded. Linkage: element types (links, pivot connectors, sliding connectors, gears, chains, splines/cams, motors/actuators). Gear Generator: object types (gear, internal gear, rack, planetary set, chain wheel set, belt wheel set) and connection types (mesh, axle). No single top-level classification of mechanisms
coverage.example_types: four-bar linkage (crank-rocker); slider-crank; Watt six-bar (Watt I, Watt II); Stephenson six-bar (I, II, III); eight-bar linkage; Theo Jansen leg linkage; Klann walking linkage; Watt straight-line linkage; Whitworth quick-return mechanism; Hoberman circle (expanding linkage); Paddington rolling bridge (curling bridge linkage); linkage aperture (iris); level-keeping parallel linkage (level-moving table); spline cam and follower; involute spur gear pair; helical, double-helical and herringbone gears; internal (ring) gear; rack and pinion; planetary (epicyclic) gear set and planetary differential; multi-stage (compound) gear reducer; roller-chain sprocket drive; timing-belt pulley drive (GT2/HTD)
coverage.making_methods: 3D printing and laser cutting (MotionGen exports STL/SVG part geometry and pairs with SnappyXO kits; Gear Generator exports STL/OBJ for printing and SVG/DXF for laser/CNC, with a 0.1-0.3 mm fit allowance tip for printed bores; Linkage exports DXF used by makers on laser cutters); robotics (MotionGen for walking robots, drawing bots and grippers); kinetic sculpture and automata (Linkage's rolling-ball sculpture lift, Keith Newstead owl-and-pussycat automaton sample); undergraduate engineering analysis (PMKS+)
coverage.item_count: Four apps. Example content: Linkage about 50 sample mechanism files; MotionGen library of at least 3 four-bar, 5 six-bar and an eight-bar template [uncertain]; PMKS+ about 5 example linkages [uncertain]; Gear Generator 6 object types, 9 ISO 606/ANSI chain sizes and 7 belt presets
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: torque-limiting: no. self-locking: no. hand-release only: no. one-way/ratchet: no. indexing/detent: no (no Geneva or ratchet elements; intermittent motion can only be drawn from links and cams [uncertain]). over-centre: indirectly (linkage simulators show toggle/dead-centre positions and branch changes, MotionGen has 'Change Branch'), but none label it. compliant: no (Linkage FAQ: no springs, no gravity, no physics). print-in-place: no. gear trains/gearboxes: yes, strongly in Gear Generator (spur, helical, herringbone, internal, rack, planetary and differential, chain and belt drives, multi-stage reducers with ratio, rpm and torque) and partly in Linkage (circular gears and chains, no racks); MotionGen and PMKS+ do not model gears [uncertain]. powered connectors: no (actuators are idealised motors only). adhesive types: no
coverage.entry_structure: Not entries but interactive models: each example is an editable, animated mechanism. Linkage sample page entries have a name, a one-line description, a .linkage2 file and a video. Gear Generator shows for each gear its diameters, contact ratio, working pressure angle and tooth forces in an info box with warnings. PMKS+ shows joint/link tables and graphs of position, velocity, acceleration and joint forces over time. MotionGen shows the linkage, coupler path and dimensions, with export to PDF
coverage.audience_level: MotionGen: school (K-12 student/teacher account types) through undergraduate and makers ('school going children, college students, makers and hobbyists, and industry practitioners'). PMKS+: undergraduate. Linkage: hobbyist and kinetic-sculpture makers, also used by engineers. Gear Generator: hobbyist to professional

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium: all four are free and visual, and animation makes motion easy to grasp, but you must already know roughly which mechanism you want; MotionGen and PMKS+ use kinematics jargon (dyads, RRPR, Watt/Stephenson, synthesis, poses); Linkage is simple but Windows-only; Gear Generator's manual is excellent and plain but assumes basic gear terms (module, pressure angle, profile shift), which it then explains
usefulness.has_images: yes (the apps draw clean 2D diagrams; Gear Generator's manual has labelled figures; Linkage pages have screenshots and a book-like drawing style)
usefulness.has_animations: yes, that is their main purpose: live, editable simulations. Gear Generator animates whole trains (turn by hand, lost-motion display) and has a 3D view; Linkage runs at 30 frames per second and exports HD video; MotionGen exports GIFs and has 2D/3D views; PMKS+ animates and graphs motion. Linkage and MotionGen also have YouTube tutorial videos
usefulness.gaps: Tools, not a reference: no explanation of when or why to choose a mechanism, no connection/latch/fastening types, no torque-limiting, ratchet, detent or compliant elements, no Geneva drive or escapement components, no springs or gravity (Linkage, and MotionGen/PMKS+ are kinematic), no 3D (spatial) linkages; Linkage lacks rack gears and runs only on Windows; Gear Generator exports cost money; MotionGen library names need jargon; link-sharing formats are app-specific
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Yes for 'try it yourself' links. Gear Generator and PMKS+ can put a whole design in a share URL (Gear Generator 'Copy share URL' stores nothing on a server; the PMKS+ README links a six-bar as an app.pmksplus.com URL), so an encyclopedia entry could link straight to a working planetary set or four-bar. Linkage sample files are stable downloads on one page (https://blog.rectorsquid.com/sample-linkage-mechanisms-2/). MotionGen has no per-example public URLs [uncertain]
usefulness.reusable_data: PMKS+ is MIT-licensed and on GitHub (code and example linkage URLs can be reused and forked). Linkage files are XML (.linkage2) and the samples are free downloads under the author's WTFPL-plus terms (allowed to use, not to resell). Gear Generator .gg3 files are JSON, but the app is proprietary. MotionGen .motiongen files and its library are proprietary. None provides a list or dataset of mechanism types
usefulness.maintained: All four were live in September 2026. Linkage: author posting Mac-port progress in June and September 2026. Gear Generator: '(C) 2014-2026', version 3. PMKS+: dependencies updated to Angular 22, contributors to 2025. MotionGen: web app live; Stony Brook info pages show '(c) 2023' and app code '(c) 2017-2023', so updates may have slowed [uncertain]; SnappyXO mode has moved to a separate app (snappyxo.io)
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: 1) Embed or link a live, editable model for each mechanism entry (share-URL designs from Gear Generator and PMKS+). 2) Gear Generator's 'warnings' style: plain messages that say what is wrong and what to change (e.g. 'Ring teeth must equal sun + 2 x planet teeth', 'Internal gear needs at least 8 more teeth than the pinion'). 3) Gear Generator's recipes ('a two-stage reducer') as worked examples in entries. 4) Linkage's sample page: one line of description, one file, one video per mechanism, a good minimal entry format. 5) Tracer/path drawing (Linkage, PMKS+, MotionGen) to show the path a point follows. 6) MotionGen's flow of 'draw the motion you want, get a linkage' (motion/path synthesis) as an advanced flow-chart endpoint. 7) Use the Watt/Stephenson naming as aliases, with plain names first
usefulness.design_rules_given: Gear Generator gives many: standard rack geometry (addendum 1 x module, dedendum 1.25 x module, root clearance 0.25 x module), pressure angles (20 degrees standard, 14.5 degrees older, 25 degrees for strength), teeth 4-400, ring must have at least 1 more (hard limit) and 8 more (practical) teeth than the pinion, planetary rules RN = SN + 2PN and (SN + RN)/n a whole number, ISO 606 sprocket tooth width 0.93-0.95 x inner width, DIN 6885 keyways, ISO 4032 nut traps, and a 0.1-0.3 mm bore allowance for printed parts. PMKS+ gives computed forces and torques. MotionGen and Linkage give dimensions only
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: Yes: all four generate custom geometry. Gear Generator is a parametric gear generator (teeth, module, pressure angle, helix, profile shift, holes, hubs). MotionGen synthesises linkage dimensions from target poses or paths and exports part shapes. PMKS+ synthesises a four-bar from 3 coupler poses. Linkage produces dimensioned parts lists and DXF outlines
usefulness.file_formats: MotionGen: STL, SVG, OBJ, PDF, GIF, image; mobile app PDF and XML; .motiongen project files. Linkage: DXF, JPEG/PNG, HD video, CSV motion-path data, .linkage2 (XML), print at 1:1. PMKS+: share URL and saved linkage file [uncertain]. Gear Generator: SVG, DXF, STL, OBJ (with paid pass), .gg3 (JSON), share URL
usefulness.terminology_value: medium: good for kinematic names (four-bar, slider-crank, Watt and Stephenson six-bars, RRRP-style joint strings, dyads, coupler, crank, rocker) and gear terms (module, diametral pitch, pressure angle, profile shift, undercut, contact ratio, backlash, lost motion, sun/planet/ring/carrier); Gear Generator's manual is a clear plain-English source for gear vocabulary; no translations
usefulness.decision_support: No selector or flow chart. Decision help is by trial: change a number and watch the result. Gear Generator shows live warnings and ratios; PMKS+ graphs forces; MotionGen solves 'which linkage gives this motion' (motion and path synthesis), which is a kind of design-time selector for linkages
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: PMKS+ is built on PMKS (Prof. Matthew I. Campbell, Oregon State University). MotionGen builds on Purwar and Ge's published synthesis research and is part of the SnappyXO Design suite (Stony Brook University and Mechanismic Inc.). Linkage users describe it as a replacement for Autodesk ForceEffect Motion (FAQ comment). Gear Generator 3 replaces Gear Generator 2 (imports its files). Overlaps: SAM, Working Model and SolidWorks (compared on the PMKS+ site), the Wolfram Demonstrations and MechSimulator sites already in this list, and many other gear generators (geardxf.com and others found by search, not checked)
